adverse_media.status: Subsequently confirmed as accurate after the 2020 collapse
adverse_media.summary: Beginning April 2015, FT Alphaville published a series questioning Wirecard's business model and accounting practices; allegations peaked in 2019 with FT investigations, whistleblower complaints and internal documents; the company denied all misconduct and called the reports fake.

KPMG's special audit was unable to verify the majority of Wirecard's 2016–2018 profits due to lack of cooperation from Wirecard and its partners; it also found long-time auditor EY failed to verify the existence of cash reserves in what appeared to be fraudulent bank statements. During the special audit Wirecard made misleading statements to investors, resulting in a criminal investigation after a BaFin referral to prosecutors.

Wirecard admitted €1.9bn in cash was 'missing' (it owed €3.2bn in debt); shares were suspended and fell almost 90%; auditor EY refused to sign off the accounts; CEO Markus Braun resigned 19 June 2020 and the company filed for insolvency on 25 June 2020.

Former CEO Markus Braun was detained on 22 June 2020 'on suspicion of accounting fraud and market manipulation', released on €5m bail, dismissed by the supervisory board on 30 June and re-arrested on 22 July 2020; other former board members were also arrested on fraud charges (pre-trial custody at Augsburg-Gablingen, later Stadelheim prison, Munich).

Former COO Jan Marsalek was dismissed with the rest of the executive team on 18 June 2020 and fled Germany; he remains the subject of an Interpol red notice for fraud, is reportedly living in Russia, and per British authorities was a Russian spy directing espionage operations across Europe, with his messages linked to Russia's GRU military intelligence (Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command: 'a significant person of interest', March 2025).
adverse_media.category: Fugitive / evasion of justice / foreign-intelligence ties

adverse_media.status: Parliamentary inquiry launched; BaFin leadership replaced
adverse_media.summary: BaFin had conducted investigations against journalists and short sellers over alleged market manipulation while taking little action against Wirecard; its president Felix Hufeld called the scandal a 'complete disaster'; the German Bundestag announced a full inquiry on 1 September 2020, and Hufeld and deputy Elisabeth Roegele left BaFin on 29 January 2021 as part of agency reform.

Insolvency administrator Michael Jaffé began dismantling the defunct group from 1 July 2020; in November 2020 the assets of the main business unit were sold to Santander Group for €100m, with North American, UK and Brazilian units sold earlier at undisclosed prices; all management-board members were released and ~730 employees laid off.
adverse_media.category: Insolvency proceedings / liquidation of the group

adverse_media.summary: Munich public prosecutors charged former CEO Markus Braun with fraud, breach of trust and accounting manipulation — offences carrying up to 15 years in prison; Braun denies wrongdoing and claims to be a victim of fraud; prosecutors accuse him of fabricating fictitious third-party transactions, and the insolvency administrator considers it proven the alleged Asian deals never took place.

The largest fraud case in post-war German history: Markus Braun and two other former executives (Oliver Bellenhaus, Stephan von Erffa) face charges of commercial gang fraud for falsifying Wirecard's financial statements since 2015, causing a €3.1bn loss to lending banks; the court (Judge Markus Födisch) appears convinced by key witness Bellenhaus; Braun and von Erffa deny the charges and could face over ten years in prison.

Munich Regional Court I ordered three former management board members — CEO Markus Braun, the former Chief Product Officer and the former CFO — to pay a total of EUR 140m damages plus interest for negligent breaches of duty (unsecured EUR 100m loan and EUR 100m Ocap bond subscription; Case No. 5 HK O 17452/21); Jan Marsalek was already under a partial default judgment for EUR 140m; claims against two former supervisory board members were dismissed for lack of causality.

output.risk_rationale: Wirecard AG screens HIGH risk. The entity is a defunct, insolvent German AG: it filed for insolvency on 25 June 2020 after admitting €1.9bn of supposed cash did not exist, and was dismantled, with its core business sold to Santander for €100m in November 2020 — the centre of the largest financial fraud in post-war German history (registration and status per GLEIF/Wikipedia). Accounting-fraud allegations date back to 2015–2019 (FT Alphaville/FT investigations, whistleblower complaints) and were corroborated by the KPMG special audit (2019–2020), which could not verify the majority of 2016–2018 profits and found that long-time auditor EY failed to verify the existence of cash reserves. The fraud spawned serious criminal exposure for its ownership and management: former CEO and largest shareholder Markus Braun (Austrian) was arrested twice (June and July 2020), charged in March 2022 with fraud, breach of trust and accounting manipulation, and remains on trial at the Munich regional court (trial since December 2022, verdict expected 2026); former COO Jan Marsalek (Austrian) is a fugitive under an INTERPOL red notice, reportedly living in Russia and described by British authorities as a Russian spy directing espionage operations across Europe — an extreme jurisdictional/integrity risk. Civil liability compounds the picture: on 5 September 2024 the Munich Regional Court I held former management board members liable for €140m plus interest for breaches of duty, with Marsalek already under a partial default judgment for the same amount. The company's collapse also triggered regulatory censure and a German parliamentary inquiry into supervisory failure (BaFin). By contrast, sanctions screening is clean: no matches for the entity or its principals on the OFAC SDN list, the UK OFSI/UK Sanctions List or the EU consolidated list (Marsalek appears only on non-sanctions law-enforcement lists), and no PEP designations beyond Markus Braun's advisory role in the Austrian Chancellery's strategy staff unit since 2017 (flagged PEP-adjacent). The combination of adjudicated accounting fraud, ongoing criminal trial, a fugitive ex-COO with Russian-intelligence ties, and confirmed insolvency makes this entity unbankable for onboarding purposes.
